kurz: What a credit rating measures, what a bond's yield spread pays for, and why ratings and spreads rarely assess risk the same way at the same time.

bloecke.md:
A credit rating is an opinion on how likely it is that a debtor will fail to make its payments. It says nothing about a security's price, its interest rate risk or its liquidity. The three agencies Moody's, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch cover practically the entire market. They are paid by the parties they rate. The issuer commissions the rating because large institutional buyers are not permitted to buy unrated bonds at all. Almost all criticism of the industry focuses on this conflict of interest. Since 2011 the European securities regulator ESMA has supervised the agencies registered in the EU.

The agencies' scales follow the same logic and differ only in notation. S&P and Fitch use AAA, AA, A, BBB, BB, B, CCC, CC and C, plus D for a default that has occurred. Moody's uses Aaa, Aa, A, Baa, Ba, B, Caa, Ca and C. Within a grade, S&P and Fitch make finer distinctions with `+` or `−`, Moody's with the numbers 1, 2 and 3. In addition there is an outlook, which often signals the direction of a change months in advance. For the price it is sometimes more important than the grade itself.

bloecke.titel: Rating scales with average default rate (S&P 1981-2008) and risk spread (Damodaran, January 2026)

bloecke.md: The most important boundary in the market runs right through the middle of this table, between BBB− (Baa3) and BB+ (Ba1). Above it lies the [[Investment grade|investment grade]] range, below it the speculative range, which the industry calls “high yield” and which is colloquially known as “junk”. Statistically the difference is small. According to the same S&P statistics, the average one-year default rate rises from 0.28% for BBB− to 0.68% for BB+. For AA to B, the table shows the values of the middle sub-grade, without plus or minus. For institutional investors, however, the step has major consequences, because indices, fund mandates and the capital rules for insurers (Solvency II) and for banks (Capital Requirements Regulation, CRR) are tied to this boundary. A downgrade by a single notch can therefore trigger sales that have nothing to do with the probability of default.
There is no statistical jump between BBB− and BB+; the boundary is a product of regulation. The price fall on crossing it is caused by forced selling, not by a newly discovered default risk.

bloecke.titel: Average one-year default rate by rating grade, 1981-2008
bloecke.unter: From AAA to BBB the default rates differ by tenths of a percentage point, from BB to CCC by orders of magnitude.

bloecke.md:
## How much the averages tell you

The values are averages over 28 years that include good and very bad periods. The average conceals how much the values fluctuate from year to year. In 2001, 44.55% of debtors in the CCC/C segment defaulted. In the AAA grade there was not a single year with a default over the entire series. A calculation based on averages therefore underestimates defaults in crisis years, that is, at the very time when they matter.

Moreover, a one-year rate cannot simply be multiplied by the maturity, but it can be projected forward. If you assume the same rate in every year, the probability of getting through the next five years without a default is (1 − default rate) to the power of five.

- For BBB (0.28% a year), the survival probability is 0.9972⁵ = 98.6%, which means a cumulative probability of default of around 1.4%.
- For BB (0.89%), survival is 95.6% and default around 4.4%.
- For B (7.28%), survival is 68.5%. Almost one in three debtors in this grade therefore defaults within five years.
- For CCC/C (22.67%), survival is 27.7% and default 72%.

With a constant rate, the calculation overstates the risk of the lower grades, because CCC debtors that do not default are usually upgraded and then carry a lower risk. The order of magnitude is still correct. Individual bonds from the speculative range are therefore very risky and only make sense as part of a portfolio.

## The spread as the price of default risk

The [[Credit spread|credit spread]] is the extra yield a bond offers over a government bond of the same maturity. It is a price that buyers and sellers have agreed on today, not a forecast. It can be broken down into three parts.

bloecke.formel:
Spread = expected loss + risk premium + liquidity premium
Expected loss = probability of default × (1 − recovery rate)
bloecke.erklaerung: The recovery rate (often simply called “recovery”) is the share of the face value that a creditor ultimately still receives in insolvency proceedings. For unsecured corporate bonds, the market convention is to assume around 40%. This is an assumption; the rate varies from case to case.
variablen: expected defaults per year, from rating statistics
share of the face value that flows back after a default
compensation for losses being uncertain and occurring in clusters
compensation for not being able to sell in a crisis
bloecke.beispiel: BB: 0.89% × (1 − 0.40) = 0.53 percentage points of expected loss

bloecke.titel: Credit spreads by risk class, 17 September 2026 (option-adjusted spread)
bloecke.unter: Only 56 basis points separate AAA and BBB, so spreads within investment grade currently differ unusually little by creditworthiness.

bloecke.md:
According to the Damodaran table, a BB bond pays 1.84 percentage points more than a US government bond. If you assume the same spread over German federal bonds, that comes to €184 of extra interest a year on €10,000. The expected loss is 0.89% × 60% × 10,000 = €53. Around €131 remains as a premium for uncertainty and illiquidity, just over 1% of the capital invested.

One grade lower, the calculation turns negative. B bonds yield 3.21 percentage points more, or €321. The expected loss according to the long-term statistics is 7.28% × 60% × 10,000 = €437. On paper, this leaves a shortfall of €116.

This does not prove that high yield is too expensive in 2026. The indices consist mainly of BB and B+ debtors, and in calm years defaults are far below the long-term average. The calculation does show, however, how little is left after deducting the expected loss when spreads are tight.

For the upper grades, the calculation works the other way round. A BBB spread of 1.11 percentage points compares with an expected loss of 0.17 percentage points. More than 0.9 percentage points are therefore paid for something other than expected defaults. In the literature this mismatch is called the credit spread puzzle. The usual explanations are that defaults occur in clusters during recessions, when losses are hardest to bear, that corporate bonds are harder to trade than government bonds, and that regulated buyers pay a premium for credit safety.

## Short-term movements in spreads

Ratings change in steps and with a delay, whereas spreads change daily and in jumps. Between 22 January 2025 (2.59 percentage points) and 7 April 2025 (4.61), the US high-yield spread widened by 78%. The trigger was a tariff shock and not a wave of insolvencies. By August 2026 the spread had fallen back to 2.70. Investors who held on to their bonds suffered price losses even though nothing had changed in the debtors' ability to pay. Buyers in April received almost twice the spread for the same credit risk.

bloecke.titel: US high-yield spread, monthly average October 2023 to August 2026
bloecke.unter: Credit risk is barely priced in for long periods and then abruptly repriced, as in April 2025, with a spread of 4.03 percentage points as a monthly average and 4.61 percentage points as a daily value on 7 April.

serien.name: ICE BofA US High Yield OAS

bloecke.md: A spread of 2.70 percentage points, as in mid-September 2026, is historically low. From this level it can fall only a little further but can rise sharply. With tight spreads, opportunities and risks are therefore unevenly distributed. Investors who buy high yield because the yield looks decent get that yield without the cushion that a wider spread would provide.

## Ratings in the 2008 financial crisis

The financial crisis was also a crisis of ratings. Securitised mortgage loans were split into tranches. The top tranche received an AAA rating because the models assumed that individual loan defaults occur largely independently of one another. This assumption proved wrong when US house prices fell nationwide at the same time. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission estimated that, of all mortgage-backed securities Moody's had rated AAA in 2006, around 73% had been downgraded to junk by April 2010. Of the AAA-rated CDOs issued between 2005 and 2007, more than half of the volume had been impaired by the end of 2009.

The economic incentives pointed in the same direction. Structured products were the growth business, and in 2007 rating these products accounted for around half of Moody's rating revenue, just under 40% of its total revenue. In addition, before commissioning a rating, the issuer could have calculations run to find out which agency would certify the most favourable structure. This does not mean that ratings are worthless. For conventional bonds they have reliably sorted risk for decades. The crisis did show, however, that the same symbol can be awarded to two completely different kinds of securities.

A rating assesses a debtor, not a financial construct. If the risk distribution comes from a model, the rating inherits the model's assumptions, including the assumption that not all loans default at the same time.

## Fallen angels and forced selling

A [[Fallen angel|fallen angel]] is a bond that was issued as investment grade and later downgraded to the speculative range. The sequence of events after such a downgrade explains why these securities often fall much further than the new probability of default justifies.

bloecke.titel: Consequences of a downgrade to fallen angel
bloecke.unter: The price loss arises in the boxes of the middle and right-hand columns, not in the first box with the downgrade itself.

knoten.notiz: IG indices and index-tracking funds may not hold the bond
Solvency II and CRR require more capital per euro of bonds
Many sellers, few buyers, thin market
The price slump exceeds the change in the probability of default
The next coupon is higher, and the rating comes under further pressure

bloecke.md:
The reverse path, from the speculative range back to investment grade, is called a rising star. It triggers the same sequence with the opposite sign, that is, forced buying and a falling spread. Prices in credit markets thus regularly result from rules for buyers, regardless of how the debtor is assessed.

## Zombie firms

According to the definition of the Bank for International Settlements, a [[Zombie firm|zombie firm]] is a company at least ten years old whose operating profit has failed to cover its interest expense for three years in a row. Its interest coverage ratio is therefore persistently below one. In 2018, Banerjee and Hofmann showed for fourteen developed countries, including Germany, that the share of such firms among listed companies had risen from around 2% in the late 1980s to about 12%. Under the narrower definition, which also requires a below-average market valuation, it rose to 6%.

As long as interest rates are at zero and spreads are tight, a company that does not earn its interest can replace every maturing bond with a new one. If both rise, the refinancing date decides whether the company survives. The ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026, and the yield on the ten-year Bund was 3.46% on 13 October 2026. The spreads in the Damodaran table refer to US government bonds. If you apply the BB spread of 1.84 percentage points to the Bund yield, a BB debtor pays around 5.3% on paper. With the same spread on the Bund yield at the end of 2021 (−0.23%), it would have been 1.6%. The difference is due entirely to the risk-free base rate; creditworthiness is unchanged in this calculation. Default rates follow this shift with a delay, because they depend on the maturity calendar and not on the timing of the rate decision.

The agencies rely mainly on four measures: the ability to cover interest expense from operating profit (interest coverage ratio); debt relative to earnings; the volatility of cash flow; and the industry, because cyclical businesses are rated lower for the same ratio. Aswath Damodaran derives a “synthetic rating” from the interest coverage ratio alone. Companies whose earnings cover their interest several times over end up at the top of the scale, those that barely cover it at the bottom.

For investors, a rating change almost never brings anything new. The market has usually adjusted the spread weeks in advance, and the agency confirms what the price is already signalling.

- A rating is useful for sorting by default risk and is not a promise of safety. It says nothing about interest rate risk. A thirty-year AAA bond, for example, loses more when interest rates rise than a two-year BB bond.
- Always compare the spread with its own historical range, not with zero. The spread only becomes meaningful when compared with what is normal in that segment.
- In the speculative range the distribution is asymmetric, with limited extra return and a possible total loss. Investments in this range therefore only work when broadly diversified through funds or ETFs, not with three individual bonds.
- In crises, high yield behaves much like equities, because spreads widen precisely when share prices are also falling. Bonds from the lower end of the scale are therefore not suitable for stabilising a portfolio.
- German federal bonds are the benchmark in the euro area. Any spread that another bond offers is the price for its difference from this benchmark.

mitnehmen: A rating ranks debtors by their probability of default; it guarantees nothing and assesses neither the price nor the interest rate risk.
Default rates do not rise linearly: from AAA to BBB they differ by tenths of a percentage point, from BB to CCC by orders of magnitude.
The spread first covers the expected loss, only the remainder is risk premium, and with a high-yield spread of 2.70 percentage points (mid-September 2026) little of it is left.
Spreads change abruptly and ratings follow with a delay; the largest price moves in the credit market are caused by forced selling at the boundary between investment grade and the speculative range.
2008 showed that a rating is only as good as the model behind it, and that economic incentives shape these models.

begriffe.text: Rating range from AAA/Aaa to BBB−/Baa3. Below it begins the speculative range (high yield). The boundary is anchored in regulation, because fund mandates, indices and the capital rules for banks and insurers are tied to it.
Extra yield of a bond over a government bond of the same maturity. It compensates for expected default losses, uncertainty and poor tradability, and fluctuates much more than actual default rates.
Probability of default multiplied by the share lost in a default (1 minus the recovery rate). This part of the spread should be treated like a provision and does not count as income.

Bond issued as investment grade and later downgraded to the speculative range. Index exclusion and regulatory selling pressure usually push the price down further than the changed probability of default explains.

By the definition of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), a company at least ten years old whose operating profit has not covered its interest expense for three years in a row. Such firms survive as long as they can refinance cheaply.
